nationality_or_literary_tradition: British-American; the thirties public poem, the elegy and the poetry of the modern city
literary_identity: Poet, dramatist and critic; the central English poet of the 1930s, the leader of the Auden generation, and one of the great public poets of the century.
biography: Born Wystan Hugh Auden in York on 21 February 1907, the son of a physician; he read at Christ Church, Oxford, where his Poems (1928, privately printed by Spender) and Poems (1930) made him the leader of his generation. The Orators (1932), Look, Stranger! (1936), the plays with Isherwood (The Dog Beneath the Skin, 1935; The Ascent of F6, 1936; On the Frontier, 1938) and Journey to a War (1939) made him the voice of the decade; he emigrated to America in 1939, became an American citizen in 1946, and returned to Oxford as professor of poetry (1956–61). He died in Vienna on 29 September 1973.
literary_profile: Auden is the central English poet of the 1930s and one of the great poets of the century: he gave the decade its public voice — the clipped, journalistic line, the parable, the political fable — and then, in America, wrote the great religious and meditative poems ('In Memory of W. B. Yeats', 'Musée des Beaux Arts', 'September 1, 1939', the Christmas oratorio For the Time Being). His technical range — ballad, sonnet, sestina, haiku, libretto, light verse — is unmatched in modern English poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: The clipped journalistic line with the flat technical vocabulary; the rhymed parable and the nursery-rhyme turned political; the catalogue of places and machines; the public elegy; the sudden turn from satire to tenderness; the colloquial idiom held in strict form.
intellectual_concerns: Totalitarianism and the coming war; class, the public school and the English ruling order; love, anxiety and the divided self; the modern city, the aeroplane and the machine; faith, the Church and the possibility of belief; history and the individual's place in it.
historical_significance: Auden is the central English poet of the period after Eliot: he gave the thirties its public voice, invented the political poem as a modern form, wrote the great elegies and meditations of the century, and his technical range made him the model for every English poet since. He is the period's most influential poet after Eliot and Yeats.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British-American; the Berlin novel, the documentary report and the autobiography of a generation
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and memoirist; the author of Goodbye to Berlin and Berlin Stories, the source of Cabaret, and the closest collaborator of Auden.
biography: Born Christopher William Bradshaw-Isherwood at Disley, Cheshire, on 26 August 1904; he read at Cambridge, left without a degree, worked as a tutor and a secretary, and went to Berlin in 1929, where he taught English and wrote The Last of Mr Norris (1935) and Goodbye to Berlin (1939). He collaborated with Auden on three plays, emigrated to America in 1939, worked in Hollywood as a screenwriter, became a Hindu monk and the disciple of Swami Prabhavananda, translated the Bhagavad Gita, and wrote the autobiographical Lions and Shadows (1938) and Christopher and His Kind (1976). He died at Santa Monica on 4 January 1986.
literary_profile: Isherwood's Berlin novels are the finest English record of the Weimar Republic's last years: Goodbye to Berlin gave the period its image of the doomed city and its narrator's famous 'I am a camera', and the two Berlin books became the musical Cabaret. His documentaries — Journey to a War with Auden, The Condor and the Cows — and his frank autobiography made him the period's great witness and one of the first English writers to write openly about homosexuality.
stylistic_characteristics: The camera-eye narration: the observer who records without comment; the flat, exact, unadorned sentence; the scene assembled from dialogue and detail; the documentary report with the novelist's eye; the self-deprecating autobiographical confidence.
intellectual_concerns: Berlin and the collapse of the Weimar Republic; the rise of the Nazis and the political emergency; the expatriate and the Englishman abroad; homosexuality and the double life; the documentary witness and the artist's responsibility; India, religion and the search for a teacher.
historical_significance: Isherwood wrote the definitive English book about Weimar Berlin and one of the great documentaries of the period: Goodbye to Berlin gave the thirties its image of the doomed city, the Berlin stories became Cabaret, and Christopher and His Kind made him a pioneer of gay autobiography.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the thirties lyric, the political poem and the poetry of the Spanish war
literary_identity: Poet, essayist and editor; one of the central poets of the Auden generation and the editor of Horizon and Encounter.
biography: Born Stephen Harold Spender in London on 28 February 1909, the son of a journalist; he read at University College, Oxford, where he printed Auden's first book, and published Twenty Poems (1930), Poems (1933), Vienna (1934) and The Still Centre (1939). He joined the Communist Party briefly in 1937, served in the National Fire Service in the war, edited Horizon with Cyril Connolly (1939–41) and Encounter (1953–67), taught at American universities, and died in London on 16 July 1995.
literary_profile: Spender is the lyric poet of the Auden generation: 'The Pylons', 'The Express', 'Not Palaces' and 'I Think Continually of Those Who Were Truly Great' are the finest poems of the thirties' public manner, and his Spanish Civil War poems gave the decade its conscience. As editor of Horizon and Encounter he made the period's literary conversation, and his autobiography World Within World is one of the great English memoirs of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The lyric line held in traditional stanza; the aeroplane, the pylon and the machine as symbols of the future; the political statement made in the first person; the elegy for the dead of Spain; the autobiographical prose of a generation.
intellectual_concerns: The thirties and the coming war; the Spanish Civil War; the machine, the pylon and the modern landscape; love, homosexuality and the private life; the artist's politics and the betrayal of the cause; memory and the lost generation.
historical_significance: Spender is one of the central poets of the Auden generation and the period's great editor: 'The Pylons' and 'Not Palaces' are the finest poems of the thirties' public style, his Spanish war poems gave the decade its conscience, and Horizon and Encounter made him the period's principal literary editor.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-British; the thirties poem of the ordinary and the elegy of the modern city
literary_identity: Poet, dramatist and radio writer; the finest poet of the Auden generation after Auden, the author of Autumn Journal, and the period's great writer for radio.
biography: Born Frederick Louis MacNeice in Belfast on 12 September 1907, the son of a clergyman; his mother died when he was six and he was sent to school in England, reading classics at Oxford and lecturing in classics at Birmingham and London. Blind Fireworks (1929), Poems (1935) and Autumn Journal (1939) made his name; he worked for the BBC from 1941 as a writer and producer of radio features, translated Aeschylus and Goethe, and died in London on 3 September 1963.
literary_profile: MacNeice is the most individual poet of the Auden generation: Autumn Journal — a long poem of the months from autumn 1938 to the spring of 1939 — is the finest poetic diary of the period, and 'Bagpipe Music', 'Snow' and 'The Sunlight on the Garden' are among the best-loved poems of the century. As a BBC writer he invented the radio feature as a literary form, and his criticism (Modern Poetry, 1938) is the sharpest account of what the thirties were doing.
stylistic_characteristics: The long conversational poem in sections; the rhyme that falls with comic exactness; the catalogue of ordinary things (the bicycle, the pub, the newspaper); the classical and the modern held side by side; the radio script's montage of voices and sound.
intellectual_concerns: The thirties and the coming war; Belfast, Ireland and the divided inheritance; the ordinary English life and the objects of the modern city; time, love and the transience of everything; the classics and the modern world; the provinces and the metropolis.
historical_significance: MacNeice wrote the finest long poem of the thirties in Autumn Journal and the best-loved lyrics of the Auden generation, invented the radio feature as a literary form, and his criticism gives the period its clearest account of itself. He is the most individual and the most durable poet of his group.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the political essay, the documentary report and the dystopian novel
literary_identity: Novelist, essayist and journalist; the greatest English political writer of the century, the author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, and the master of the modern essay.
biography: Born Eric Arthur Blair at Motihari, Bengal, on 25 June 1903, the son of an opium department official; he was educated at Eton, served in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma (1922–27), lived in poverty in London and Paris, and published Down and Out in Paris and London (1933), Burmese Days (1934), The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) and Homage to Catalonia (1938). He fought in the Spanish Civil War and was shot through the throat; he wrote for the Tribune and the Observer, broadcast for the BBC, and published Animal Farm (1945) and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949). He died of tuberculosis in London on 21 January 1950.
literary_profile: Orwell is the greatest English political writer of the period: his essays ('Politics and the English Language', 'Shooting an Elephant', 'Why I Write') are the finest in the language, The Road to Wigan Pier is the great documentary of the Depression, Homage to Catalonia the finest English book on the Spanish war, and Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four the two most influential political fables ever written in English. He made plain prose a moral instrument.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain declarative English sentence with no ornament; the essay built as an argument that turns on an example; the documentary detail and the transcribed testimony; the fable and the allegory (Animal Farm); the invented political vocabulary (Newspeak, doublethink); the honesty that records what it would rather not.
intellectual_concerns: Totalitarianism, propaganda and the corruption of language; poverty, unemployment and the English class system; empire and the colonial servant; the Spanish Civil War and the betrayal of the revolution; the individual against the state; the honest record against the lie.
historical_significance: Orwell is the greatest English political writer of the century and the period's central essayist: Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four are the most influential political fables in English, The Road to Wigan Pier and Homage to Catalonia are permanent documentaries, and his essays made plain prose a moral instrument. His vocabulary — Big Brother, doublethink, Newspeak, thoughtcrime — has entered the world's political language.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the novel of ideas, the dystopia and the essay of the modern consciousness
literary_identity: Novelist, essayist and mystic; the author of Brave New World, the most influential English dystopia, and the period's most wide-ranging essayist.
biography: Born Aldous Leonard Huxley at Godalming, Surrey, on 26 July 1894, the grandson of T. H. Huxley and the grand-nephew of Matthew Arnold; an eye disease blinded him temporarily and ended his medical ambitions, and he read English at Oxford. Crome Yellow (1921), Antic Hay (1923), Those Barren Leaves (1925) and Point Counter Point (1928) made him the wittiest novelist of the twenties; Brave New World followed in 1932, Eyeless in Gaza in 1936 and After Many a Summer in 1939. He moved to California in 1937, wrote The Perennial Philosophy (1945) and The Doors of Perception (1954), and died in Los Angeles on 22 November 1963.
literary_profile: Huxley wrote the most influential English dystopia and the wittiest novel of ideas of the period: Brave New World is the century's great warning about engineered happiness, Point Counter Point is the finest English novel of the twenties' intellectual world, and his essays (Music at Night, Ends and Means, The Perennial Philosophy) made science, mysticism and politics the subjects of a brilliant prose. He is the period's most encyclopaedic intelligence.
stylistic_characteristics: The novel of ideas with a large cast and competing arguments; the witty epigram and the satirical portrait à clef; the documentary insert and the newspaper clipping (Point Counter Point); the expository essay carried by image and analogy; the dystopian world described through its own propaganda.
intellectual_concerns: The future, science and the engineered society; pleasure, drugs and the managed mind; the intellect against the body; mysticism and the perennial philosophy; the twenties' smart set and its boredom; overpopulation, ecology and the limits of progress.
historical_significance: Huxley wrote the most influential English dystopia and the finest novel of ideas of the period: Brave New World is a permanent warning about technology and happiness, Point Counter Point is the definitive novel of the twenties' intellectual world, and his essays made science and mysticism the matter of a great prose. He is the period's most encyclopaedic mind.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the comic novel of the twenties, the Catholic novel and the war trilogy
literary_identity: Novelist, biographer and travel writer; the greatest English comic novelist of the century and the author of Decline and Fall, Brideshead Revisited and Sword of Honour.
biography: Born Arthur Evelyn St John Waugh in London on 28 October 1903, the son of a publisher; he read at Oxford, failed to settle to anything, taught in Wales and travelled in the Mediterranean, and made his name with Decline and Fall (1928) and Vile Bodies (1930). He converted to Catholicism in 1930, published A Handful of Dust (1934), Scoop (1938), Brideshead Revisited (1945) and the Sword of Honour trilogy (1952–61), and wrote the finest English travel books of the period. He died at Combe Florey, Somerset, on 10 April 1966.
literary_profile: Waugh is the greatest English comic novelist of the century: Decline and Fall and Vile Bodies invented the twenties' comic manner, A Handful of Dust is one of the darkest novels in English, Brideshead Revisited is the period's great elegy for the Catholic aristocracy, and Sword of Honour is the finest English novel of the Second World War. His prose — exact, sonorous, merciless — is the period's most perfect comic instrument.
stylistic_characteristics: The comedy of the absurd with a perfectly straight face; the sentence that ends in a catastrophe delivered as an aside; the catalogue of eccentric characters; the travel book's comic encounter; the Catholic novel's structure of grace and vocation; the elegy for the great house.
intellectual_concerns: The twenties' smart set and its empty pleasures; the English aristocracy and the great house; Catholicism, grace and the vocation; the Second World War and the comedy of the army; the empire and the English abroad; death, judgement and the failure of the world.
historical_significance: Waugh is the greatest English comic novelist of the century and the period's finest prose stylist: Decline and Fall and Vile Bodies made the comic novel modern, A Handful of Dust and Brideshead Revisited are permanent, and Sword of Honour is the finest English novel of the Second World War.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the fair-play detective novel and the puzzle plot
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the best-selling novelist of all time, the creator of Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple, and the central figure of the Golden Age of detective fiction.
biography: Born Agatha Mary Clarissa Miller at Torquay on 15 September 1890; she trained as a pharmacist and dispenser during the First World War, which gave her the poisons that fill her plots, and published The Mysterious Affair at Styles in 1920. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926), Murder on the Orient Express (1934) and And Then There Were None (1939) made her the most popular writer in the world; The Mousetrap (1952) became the longest-running play in history. She was made a Dame in 1971 and died at Wallingford, Oxfordshire, on 12 January 1976.
literary_profile: Christie perfected the fair-play detective novel and is the best-selling novelist of all time: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd is the most audacious solution in the genre, And Then There Were None the most mathematically elegant, and her stage play The Mousetrap the longest-running in the world. She made the puzzle plot a form of art, and her two detectives — Poirot and Marple — are among the most famous characters in fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The fair-play plot with its clues planted in plain sight; the closed circle of suspects; the misdirection and the double bluff; the flat functional prose that never distracts from the mechanism; the final explanation scene in which the detective assembles the truth.
intellectual_concerns: Murder in the closed community; the English village and the country house; money, wills and the family; the servant, the foreigner and the outsider as suspect; the English order restored; the psychology of concealment.
historical_significance: Christie is the best-selling novelist of all time and the central figure of the Golden Age: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd and And Then There Were None are the most perfectly constructed detective novels in English, The Mousetrap is the longest-running play in the world, and her two detectives are permanent characters of the culture.
